Define intake as a versioned, tenant-configurable question graph (JSON schema): question, answer type, branching rules, required flag, FEMA/PDA field mapping, translations.
Present one question at a time on every channel; group only questions research shows belong together (e.g. street + city).
Branch so people see only relevant questions: renters never see owner-only questions; flood shows waterline questions; wind shows roof questions.
Median completion for a basic damage report ≤ 5 minutes on a mid-range phone over 3G; target ≤ 12 required questions on the shortest path.
Every closed question offers "I don't know" and "Skip" where the field is not legally required; neither blocks submission.
Show progress as steps remaining in words ("About 4 questions left"), not a percentage bar that jumps with branching.
Ask the safety screen first: "Is anyone in danger right now?" A yes shows local emergency instructions (ACC-48) before anything else.
Write questions at or below grade 5 reading level, measured automatically in CI and reviewed by a person.
Damage-level questions use plain descriptions with illustrations, never FEMA terms: "Can you still safely live in your home?" rather than "Is the residence habitable?"
Each question shows one short example answer and why it is asked ("This helps us send the right volunteers").
Use picture-choice answers for damage type (roof, windows, water inside, tree on house, home moved off foundation).
At any point a resident may type or speak freely ("A tree fell on the back bedroom and water came in"). AI extracts candidate answers for later questions.
AI-extracted answers are shown back as plain statements for one-tap confirm or edit ("You said: tree on house — is that right?"). Unconfirmed extractions are never saved as answers.
Questions already answered by a confirmed extraction are skipped; the review screen still lists them.
Store the resident's original words verbatim alongside extracted fields, in the original language.
If AI is unavailable, the same graph runs without it (ACC-37, CMD-05).
Calm, warm, non-clinical tone. No exclamation marks, emoji, gamification or celebratory animations.
Never ask why someone did not evacuate, insure, or prepare. Never imply blame.
Questions about household members, disability, medical needs or immigration-adjacent topics are optional, explain their purpose, and are asked after the damage report is safely saved.
Offer a "Pause" that saves a draft with a short resume code, respecting shared-device rules (ACC-41).
Before submit, show a plain-language summary grouped into "Your home," "What happened," "What you need," each editable.

Confirmation gives a short human-readable reference (e.g. 4 letters + 4 digits, no ambiguous characters), sent by SMS or email if the person chose that, and states what happens next without promising aid (ACC-30).

Ask for a guided shot list based on hazard type: (1) whole home from outside, (2) worst damage close-up, (3) for flood, the highest waterline with a common object for scale, (4) optional interior. Mirrors what counties already ask residents for.
Show an illustrated example for each requested shot, plus a safety line: "Do not go inside if it is unsafe."
On-device checks before upload (blur, darkness, nothing building-like in frame) give one plain retake suggestion. Run in the browser where possible so it works on slow connections.
Photos are optional for submission. A report without photos is valid and is routed for field verification.
Accept photos from the camera or gallery, and SMS/MMS on the SMS channel; compress client-side to a tenant-set size (default ≤ 1.5 MB).
Read GPS and time from EXIF only to suggest location and date for the resident to confirm, then strip all EXIF from stored derivatives.
Detect and blur faces, license plates and visible documents in any image shown outside the reviewing case worker role. Keep the original in restricted storage.
Never publish public-submitted photos to public dashboards by default.

AI produces, per report: a suggested FEMA degree of damage (affected, minor, major, destroyed, or "cannot tell"), a confidence score, and the visible features behind it ("roof covering missing," "waterline above outlets").
Suggestions are labeled "AI suggestion — not verified" everywhere they appear and are never shown to the resident as a finding (ACC-11).
A credentialed reviewer sets the official degree of damage. Record suggestion, decision, reviewer and whether they agreed.

Use a purpose-trained or fine-tuned image classifier, evaluated against FEMA matrix labels, for the suggestion. A general-purpose vision-LLM may describe features and check photo quality, but may not supply the severity rating. Source the model through a university research partnership that supplies FEMA-matrix-labeled images, independent validation and a published model card; keep the model behind a swappable inference interface.

Before launch and per model version, publish accuracy by hazard type, home type (conventional vs manufactured) and neighborhood income band. Do not ship a model that is materially less accurate for any group.
Sort the review queue by need signals (people unsafe, no shelter, medical needs) first and AI severity second, so AI never pushes vulnerable households down.
Flag possible duplicates by address, near-identical images and reverse-image matches to known stock or prior-event photos, for human review only.

Export reviewed reports in a format that supports state Initial Damage Assessment and FEMA desktop PDA packages: counts by degree of damage, home type, owner/renter, insured status, representative photos, and map layer.
One report record regardless of channel; record channel of origin and every channel used.
Mobile web is a PWA: no account or install required, installable optionally, works on the two most recent major versions of iOS Safari and Android Chrome plus 4-year-old devices.
SMS: a keyword (e.g. DAMAGE / DANOS) starts the flow in the matching language; numbered answers; "BACK," "SKIP," "HELP," "STOP" always work; MMS photos attach to the current question.
SMS carrier compliance: registered sender (10DLC or toll-free verified), STOP/HELP handling, no marketing content.
IVR offers speech or keypad answers in each launch language and transfers to a live agent at any point; agents work in a staff view of the same flow.
Assisted mode records the helper, the affected person and their consent (ACC-46); helper sees only what they entered, and the session clears on completion.
Assisted/kiosk mode captures reports offline with encrypted local storage, shows "Not sent yet" until the server confirms, and syncs with duplicate protection (ACC-39).
QR codes and short URLs on flyers and door hangers open the flow pre-set to the tenant, event and language.
Residents can switch channels mid-report using their reference code (start by SMS, add photos on web).

After the damage report saves, ask: "Do you need help with any of these?" — shelter tonight, food or water, cleanup or tarp, medical equipment or power, transportation, pets, someone to talk to. Multi-select with icons.
Needs are a separate record linked to the damage report, so a household can ask for help without reporting damage and vice versa.

Consent screen names each receiving organization type in plain words ("Volunteer cleanup groups like Salvation Army or local churches") with yes/no per type. Default is no sharing. Damage reporting to the emergency manager is never conditional on sharing consent (ACC-45).
Partners receive only the minimum fields for their service (a cleanup crew gets address, need, contact preference — not income, medical or household details).
Residents can withdraw consent by SMS or web using their reference code; partners are notified and access is revoked within 1 hour.
Show nearby approved resources (shelters, PODs, cooling/warming centers) from tenant-published data only, with "last updated" time; never invent availability (CMD example in 10.8).
Export needs to partner case-management systems via documented API and CSV, and support multi-agency "who is handling this" claim-and-release to avoid duplicate visits.
Spiritual and emotional care is offered as an optional need, phrased without assuming any faith ("Would you like someone to talk with — a counselor or a chaplain?").
Do not ask about citizenship, immigration status, criminal history or income in the intake. If a tenant program legally requires income, it is a separate optional step with a stated reason.
Treat renters, mobile-home residents, multi-generational households and people experiencing homelessness as primary personas; every flow is tested with them before release.
Never require proof of ownership, ID, SSN, insurance or a bank account to submit a report or a need.
Accept any address form: apartment/unit, rural route, landmark description, "no fixed address," and Unicode names (ACC-36).
Imagery and examples show diverse homes (apartments, manufactured homes, rural, urban) and people, reviewed by community members.
Faith-neutral by default; tenants may add faith-based partners, always as an opt-in choice.

Launch with English and Spanish (decided 2026-10-12). Later languages come from tenants' Census language data, drawing on Chinese, Vietnamese, Tagalog, Arabic, Korean, Russian, Haitian Creole, French and Hindi. The product is built so adding a language needs no code change.

All fixed strings (questions, errors, consent, confirmation) are professionally translated and community-reviewed per language before that language goes live; machine translation is not acceptable for fixed strings (ACC-35).
Free text and voice may be in any language; store the original, show reviewers a labeled machine translation, and never decide eligibility on the translation alone.
Right-to-left layout for Arabic and any other RTL language enabled.
Language is detected from the device and from a first-screen picker showing each language in its own script; SMS keywords exist in each language.
Equity dashboard per event: report and need rates by census tract compared to tract population, renter share, income and language, to spot under-reporting areas for outreach.
Track time-to-review and time-to-help by tract income band, renter vs owner, language and channel; alert when gaps exceed a tenant-set threshold.
Demographic questions are optional, asked after submission, and used only in aggregate (minimum cell size 11) for equity reporting.
Co-design and usability test with community organizations representing low-literacy, LEP, disability, older adult and renter groups each release, compensating participants.
Build to NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 Moderate from day one: system security plan, control inheritance from the cloud provider, continuous monitoring.
Pursue GovRAMP Ready, then Authorized, with a 3PAO; pursue SOC 2 Type II in parallel.
Map data handling to state breach-notification laws in every tenant state, starting with Missouri.
Support HIPAA-aligned handling (BAA-capable providers) for the medical-needs fields, even where HIPAA does not strictly apply.

Multi-tenant with strict tenant isolation enforced in the database (row-level security keyed to tenant) and in object storage (per-tenant prefixes and keys); automated tests prove no cross-tenant read.
Role- and attribute-based access: role, organization, event, geography and data category all gate access. Default deny.
Staff sign-in via tenant SSO (SAML/OIDC) with phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2/passkeys preferred); no shared accounts.
Break-glass access for emergencies is time-boxed, justified, and alerts the tenant security contact.
Residents never need an account; report lookup uses reference code plus a one-time code to the contact they gave (ACC-43).
Encrypt in transit (TLS 1.2+, HSTS) and at rest (AES-256) with per-tenant keys in a managed KMS; field-level encryption for contact details, medical needs, household composition and free-text.
Data classification on every field (public, internal, sensitive, restricted) drives storage, export, logging and AI-context rules.

Criminal-justice information (law-enforcement mission fields, suspect roles, weapons, arrest dispositions, bodycam references) is stored only in a separately authorized enclave, built for launch (own account/subscription, network boundary, keys and identity) meeting the current FBI CJIS Security Policy (v6.x), with its own MFA, audit and personnel screening ([CJIS v6.1 summary](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fbis-cjis-v61-what-security-teams-need-to-know/amp/)).

Tenant-configurable retention per data category with automated deletion. When a tenant sets none, photos, free text and other records are kept 7 years (decided 2026-10-12). Exceptions: scribe audio is deleted once the note is confirmed (FL-04), live position trails after 30 days (DSP-08), personal command conversations after 30 days, and CJIS data follows CJIS and state records rules. Legal holds override deletion; public-records request export that redacts restricted fields.
Data residency in US regions only; no resident data used to train any model without a tenant's written opt-in.
Secure SDLC: threat model per feature, SAST/DAST/dependency and container scanning in CI, signed builds, SBOM per release.
Annual third-party penetration test plus a public vulnerability disclosure policy.
Abuse protection without CAPTCHAs that block disabled users (ACC-44): rate limits, risk scoring, SMS verification only when risk is high.
Immutable, tamper-evident audit log of every read of restricted data, export, permission change and AI action (CMD-37), retained per tenant policy.
Incident response plan with tenant notification within contractually defined hours, tested twice a year.
Maintain an AI use register: each AI feature, model and version, provider, data sent, decision it informs, human checkpoint, and owner.
Resident free text, photos, and partner notes are untrusted data. They are passed to models in delimited data fields and can never change system instructions, tools or permissions (CMD-11).
Resident-facing AI has no tools that read other records. Extraction returns only a fixed JSON schema, validated server-side before display.
Staff-facing AI actions go through the CMD action catalog with server-side authorization; the model holds no credentials (CMD-12, CMD-21).
Redact or tokenize names, phone numbers and exact addresses before sending text to external models where the task does not need them.
Use AI providers under enterprise terms with zero data retention and no training on customer data, in US regions; record this per provider.
Output filtering: block generated text that states eligibility, promises aid, gives medical or legal advice, or contains another person's data.

Evaluation suite run on every model or prompt change: extraction accuracy on a labeled multilingual set (including low-literacy phrasing and code-switching), prompt-injection tests, and photo-model fairness slices (PHO-13). Release blocks on regression.

Monitor in production: extraction correction rate by language, reviewer agreement rate with photo suggestions, and complaints. Auto-disable a feature per tenant when its error rate crosses a threshold, falling back to non-AI flow.
Tell residents plainly when AI is helping ("A computer helped fill in these answers — please check them") and let them turn it off for the session.
Align governance documentation with NIST AI RMF so government buyers can reuse it in procurement reviews.

AI providers are pluggable (decided 2026-10-12): one internal interface each for language models, speech-to-text, translation and image analysis, with the provider chosen per tenant in configuration. A provider can be enabled only if it meets AIG-06 (US processing, zero data retention, no training on customer data) and passes the evaluation suite (AIG-08) for that tenant's languages. Switching providers needs no code change, and every AI output records which provider and model produced it.

Tenant hierarchy: state → region/coalition → county/city → partner organization, with data-sharing agreements modeled explicitly between tenants (e.g. county shares de-identified counts with state, full records with its VOAD only when consented).
Events (incidents) are first-class: each report belongs to one or more events; tenants open an event, publish its intake link/keyword, and close it.
Handle a surge of 50,000 report submissions per hour across tenants and 10,000 concurrent SMS sessions, with intake writes queued so submission never fails under load. Load-test to 2×.
Photo uploads go direct to object storage with resumable uploads; processing is asynchronous and never blocks submission.
Availability: intake 99.95% monthly; staff console 99.9%. Multi-AZ by default, warm standby in a second US region with RPO ≤ 15 minutes and RTO ≤ 1 hour.
Graceful degradation order when dependencies fail: AI features off → photo processing deferred → maps off → intake still accepts text reports.
Infrastructure as code for every environment; per-tenant configuration (questions, languages, partners, branding, retention) without code changes.
White-label per tenant (logo, colors, domain, sender name), meeting contrast rules (ACC-08) regardless of brand colors.
Standards-based integrations: Esri ArcGIS feature services for PDA maps, CSV/GeoJSON export, webhooks, and a documented REST API with per-tenant keys and scopes.

Portable containers from day one. Every service runs in Docker, started locally with one Docker Compose command on Docker Desktop. Cloud services sit behind adapters with local stand-ins so the same images later run in a government cloud without code changes: PostgreSQL with PostGIS for data, S3-compatible storage (MinIO locally), a secrets and key service (a local vault in development, the cloud's key management service in production), and a standard message queue. Configuration comes only from environment variables and secrets, never from code.

Development rules until the move: only synthetic or exercise data on laptops, never real resident or criminal-justice data. The CJIS enclave is built and tested as its own separate container set, but holds real data only after it moves to an authorized government cloud and passes the state CJIS audit. Twilio and other webhooks reach a laptop only through a secured development tunnel.

Maps are open source: MapLibre for display on web and in the React Native field app, with OpenStreetMap data. Map tiles and address search (geocoding) are self-hosted in containers, because OpenStreetMap's free public tile servers are not for production use. Counties' parcel data is loaded per tenant. Offline map packages for the field app are cut from the self-hosted tiles. Esri ArcGIS and FEMA field tools are still supported through import and export (CON-17, SCL-09), not as the base map.

Release 1 includes every requirement in this document (decided 2026-10-12). Claude Code builds it in this order so each layer stands on a tested one: (1) platform foundations: tenancy, identity, permissions, audit, save and retry rules (FR-00, SEC); (2) resident intake on web, text and phone, review queue and verification; (3) needs board, partner sharing and public "Find help"; (4) missions, dispatch board and the React Native field app; (5) CJIS enclave; (6) FEMA package and official reports; (7) AI features: scribe, photo pre-sort, recommendations, resource discovery and the command window; (8) ICS forms and EOC functions. Every layer must pass its acceptance cases and the original launch gates before the next starts.

Claude Code records each technology choice (language, frameworks, database, queue, React Native libraries) in a short decision record in the repository: what was chosen, the alternatives, and why it fits SCL-11 and the government-cloud move.

Licensing and metering: each contract is an annual subscription per jurisdiction, tiered by population served. Store tier, term and covered jurisdictions per tenant; a state or coalition contract can cover member jurisdictions. Never meter or cap resident reports — intake stays open during any surge regardless of plan.

Add to the question graph, each with "I don't know": home type (house, apartment or condo, mobile or manufactured home, other); primary residence (yes/no); insurance covering this damage (home or renters, flood, none, not sure); cause (wind or tornado, flood, fire, other); for flood, highest water inside the living space (none, under 18 inches, 18 inches or more, to the roofline); staying somewhere else tonight; and two optional items asked after submission: anyone hurt or missing, and anyone who lost work that regular unemployment will not cover.
Residents never pick a FEMA degree of damage. Reviewers set it using the FEMA matrix for the home type, informed by answers, photos and the AI suggestion.

Every report carries a verification status: self-reported, desktop-verified (photos sufficient), field-verified, or cannot verify. Only verified reports count toward degree-of-damage totals; self-reported counts are shown separately.
Exclude pre-existing damage and non-primary residences from IA totals while keeping them in the record.
Totals by jurisdiction, tract and event, with a damage-concentration map layer.
Automatically attach the ACS population profile for affected tracts and jurisdictions; never ask residents for this.

Infrastructure outage log: facility or service type (hospital, water, wastewater, police, fire/EMS, school, child care, eldercare, roads, power), start and restoration time, flagging outages over 72 hours.
Casualty counts entered only by authorized staff from official sources; resident answers are flagged as unconfirmed.
Summarize resources committed by partners (meals, shelters, cleanup teams, donated goods) from the needs and partner records.

Public damage module for staff: site, category of work (debris, emergency protective measures, roads and bridges, water control, buildings, utilities, parks), estimated cost and photos, rolled up against the state and county per-capita indicators the tenant enters.

One-click IDA package per event and jurisdiction: IA counts by degree of damage, split by owner/renter, insured/uninsured, home type and verification status; representative photos; map; outage log; population profile; partner resources; PA cost summary; and the as-of time.

Primary output is FEMA's own PDA formats from \[fema.gov/pda\](https://www.fema.gov/sites/default/files/documents/fema\_rd\_pda-guide\_07012025.pdf): the IA Street Sheet and IA Survey (single-family and multi-family) fields, the Home Insurance Matrix categories, the PA Site Sheet and PA cost survey, and a GIS layer compatible with FEMA's field validation tools (FACT, ArcGIS Field Maps). Export to PDF, Excel/CSV and GeoJSON. Optional per-state template mappings sit on top.
The package contains counts and representative evidence only, with no personally identifiable information, matching FEMA's PDA guidance, unless a data-sharing agreement requires more.

Draft the data-driven parts of [FEMA Form 010-0-13](https://www.fema.gov/sites/default/files/documents/completing-fema-form_010-0-13.pdf), the governor's declaration request: Box 7 incident period and type, Box 8 damage description (≤3,000 characters), Box 9 resources committed (≤3,000 characters), Box 10 joint PDA dates and areas, Box 11 requested areas, and the data for Enclosure A (IA) and Enclosure B (PA). Drafts are labeled for state review; the platform never submits the form.
Keep FEMA form mappings versioned and updatable without a code release, since FEMA updates PDA forms frequently. Show which FEMA form version each export used.
Track the 30-day filing window for a major disaster request from the incident end date and show it on the event dashboard.
Every public channel reads from the site and resource records in the console (CON-09). A change reaches every channel within 2 minutes.

Each public site shows: name, address and directions, type, status (open, limited, full, closed), hours, services, pets, accessibility, power for medical devices, languages spoken, nearest transit, and when it was last confirmed.
A site not reconfirmed within a tenant-set number of hours is hidden on every channel. Site leads get a reminder before that happens.
When a site is full or closed, every channel points to the next nearest open site of the same type.
Confidential sites, including domestic violence shelters, are never published. Staff refer people to them privately.
Nothing goes public without a named person's approval. Safety-critical text is human-translated or human-reviewed (ACC-35). The log records what was published, where and when.

Public "Find help" page: no sign-in, under 300 KB first load, English and Spanish (more later), Section 9 accessible, list first with an optional map, searchable by address, ZIP or landmark, and printable.
Text a keyword in any launch language (e.g. SHELTER, REFUGIO) with a ZIP code or address and get the three nearest open sites with hours, pets and accessibility.
The phone line reads the nearest open sites in the caller's language and can transfer to a person.
Live feed to local 211 call centers and other directories in the Open Referral (HSDS) format, plus a documented API.
Drafts alert text sized for Wireless Emergency Alerts and the county's mass-notification system. The county sends it through its own authorized alert tool.
Drafts social media posts and simple graphics for each site change, ready for the PIO to approve and post.
Media sheet for TV, radio and newspapers: a page and PDF that refresh themselves, with "last updated" times.

Audio scripts, plus optional text-to-speech audio files, in several languages: a loop for a low-power AM Travelers' Information Station, and a read-out for ARES/RACES nets serving areas without cell service.
One-tap printable posters and flyers per language: large type, phone number, short web address and QR code. The QR code is never the only way in (ACC-50).
Copy-and-paste widget for city, school and partner websites.
Public open data feed (GeoJSON and HSDS) for news outlets and mapping apps, without confidential sites.

Published resources beyond sites (hotlines, programs, deadlines such as FEMA registration) are human-reviewed, in accessible HTML, and checked for accessibility when they link outside (ACC-49, ACC-51).

Staff request intake for phone and walk-in requests (dispatcher/call-taker persona): caller, callback number, language, interpreter need, location with unknowns allowed, summary and hazards, captured in under a minute. Draft-save, intake-save and dispatch prerequisites are separate (FR-02.02). The command window can draft from a spoken summary.

Hazards on every mission, dispatch card and field assignment (F04): critical hazards shown apart from the narrative; reported, confirmed, corrected and cleared kept separate; sensitive details restricted. The field app warns a team about known hazards before arrival.

Witness reporting (public role E): intake asks "Is this your home?" A "no" path records a third-party observation, asks only what was seen, never presents it as owner-confirmed, and counts it separately.
Family and caregiver helpers in the public flow (public role D): the record keeps the helper and the person they represent separate; what the helper can see later follows DEC-10.
One record of people involved per mission (F07, D07), with restricted fields. All D07 roles are supported; law-enforcement roles and details are stored in the CJIS enclave (SEC-12).
Accounts stay separate from personnel records (FR-01.05). A volunteer checked in by QR code gets a personnel record without needing a staff account.
Publish an accessibility statement and support contact on the public "Find help" page (ACC-03, FR-A10).
Moving data from the current ARK apps follows MIG-01 to MIG-09, including conservative mapping of old approval flags.
The original MET-01 to MET-10 join the Section 19 metrics.

A mission is any unit of field work: welfare check, verification route, cleanup work order, delivery, outreach sweep, site staffing. Missions exist only inside an activated disaster event (SCL-02), since the product is for disasters only (DEC-01). Every dispatch assignment (DSP-04) and need claim (CON-08) is a mission with an immutable ID and a unique human-readable reference that is never reused (FR-02.01, FR-02.04).
Mission states follow the original: draft, open, en route, on scene, cleared, closed, and reopen with a reason. Allowed skips and cancellations follow approved policy (B6, DEC-06).
Priority changes, closure and reopening need a reason and confirmation (RULE-14). Locks apply to manual and command changes equally (RULE-05).
Assigning or releasing people updates the mission and each person's assignment in one transaction (FR-06.02).

Personnel records hold recorded skills, credentials with expiry and verification, agency, department and availability, with duty, availability and response kept separate (FR-05.03). The system never infers a qualification.
Assignment conflicts warn before saving: double-booked, off duty, over an hours limit, or missing a required credential, with authorized override and reason (FR-06.03).

Badges with photo, name, agency, role, credentials and a scannable code for check-in (FLD-03) and checkpoints (FR-03). The code is never the only identification (AC-13C). Badges expire and can be revoked at once.
Badge states follow F13 (generated, print requested, print confirmed, print failed), plus an optional "handed out."
Reminders follow F09. Examples here: re-confirm a site, call back a survivor, renew a shelter agreement.
Contacts follow F17, plus 24-hour numbers, backups, and re-verification before each season.
Situation reports, briefings and the FEMA package follow F15: draft, reviewed, issued, immutable snapshots, amendments.
Administration follows F01 and F18: users, roles, partner organizations, data-sharing agreements, event templates, question graphs, planning factors, languages and branding, all audited.
A partner organization can be invited, sign its data-sharing agreement, set up users and assets, and be active in under one day.

The product name is a single configuration value, PRODUCT\_NAME, currently "Common Ground". Every place the product names itself reads it: screens, page titles, emails, help text, exports, the public "Find help" page footer and the accessibility statement. The name is never hardcoded, and changing it needs no code release. Resident texts and calls use the county's name, not the product name (SMS and phone setup tab).

Permissions are fully configurable by each county (decided 2026-10-12, original DEC-05). The product ships default role templates built from the cast, field, frontline and original A7 roles; a county administrator can copy, edit, create and assign roles by action, record scope and data category. Every change is versioned and audited, and a "what can this role do" preview shows the effect before saving.

Guardrails no county can configure away: default deny and server-side checks (FR-00.01); public users never see private records (FR-00.02); criminal-justice data only for CJIS-qualified users (SEC-12); no one approves their own finding without a policy exception that is audited (A7); no role can edit or delete audit records (FR-08.04); granting permissions needs a second administrator (Section 30.2); restricted health, counseling and legal fields stay limited to their roles (FR-15, FR-16, FR-23).
Residents check status with their reference code plus a one-time code and can change consent at any time. A reference code alone never retrieves private data (RULE-17).
Residents can correct, add to or withdraw a report. Changes after approval go to re-review (RULE-09); the original stays in the history.
Optional accommodation requests, never asking for a diagnosis, restricted to the access and functional needs coordinator (RULE-16, ACC-47).
Landlords, businesses, nonprofits and faith communities can report several properties at once; each property becomes its own record (public roles B and F).
One console with role-based workspaces (the cast table). Role, organization, event, geography and data category decide what each person sees (SEC-06).

Event templates by hazard (tornado, flood, winter storm, wildfire) preset map layers, intake questions, public messages and keywords. A new event can be opened and intake published in under 5 minutes.

Situational awareness map with layers for reports, danger flags, verified damage, needs, outages, road closures, open sites, damage footprint and Census profile. Each layer shows its source and as-of time. Everything on the map has a list equivalent (ACC-07).
A key-counts panel with as-of time: reports, unique homes, verified homes by degree of damage, displaced households, needs open/claimed/done, and sites open.
Review queue plus field-team routing. Field teams use a mobile app that works offline and syncs verification results.
"What changed since the last briefing" view and a sourced situation-report draft (CMD-16).

Reporting-coverage alerts compare reports with the structure inventory inside the damage footprint (for example FEMA's USA Structures data or county parcels). Areas below a tenant threshold are flagged as under-reported, with suggested outreach.
Needs board shared by partners: claim, assign, release and done, with overlap warnings. Partners see only consented fields (NED-04).
Site management: open, update capacity and close shelters, feeding stops, PODs and MARCs. Publishing a site updates the resident "where to get help" list (NED-06).

Danger flags are for awareness only at launch and clearly labeled "Not dispatched" (CMD-19). Decided 2026-10-12: no hand-off to 911 dispatch. When a resident answers yes to danger, they are told on screen, by SMS and on the phone line to call 911 now; the staff flag records "Resident told to call 911" with the time.
Briefing mode for the EOC wall display: large type, auto-refresh, no personal details.
The command window (Section 10) works in every workspace.

The console replaces these EOC functions, so counties need not run WebEOC or a similar system for them: damage and needs tracking; resource requests to the state (ICS 213RR fields, exportable to the state's system); situation reports and briefings (ICS 201-style incident briefing); and a significant events log with ICS 214 activity logs and ICS 213 general messages. Every record exports to PDF and CSV, and an API lets a state system that still runs WebEOC receive them.

Live conditions from three sources, each labeled with source and age: utility outage and state DOT road-closure feeds where available; Waze for Cities (two-way: receive closures and hazards, publish county closures) and Google Maps Platform for routing and travel times; and staff entry as the fallback and override.

Needs-board visibility is configurable by role, agency or individual person: who sees which partners' claims, statuses and details. Defaults follow consent rules (NED-04), and an administrator can override per event.
Shelter registration in the console for county- and NGO-run shelters (household, access needs, pets, check-in/out), plus import of shelter counts from the Red Cross system without personal details.
The field app works offline, uses the FEMA damage matrices, and syncs both ways with Esri ArcGIS (Survey123, Field Maps) and FEMA field validation tools.

Facility registry, maintained year-round, with the attributes listed in "How the console recommends." County EM approves entries; facility owners update their own details; the COAD can propose entries; facilities can self-register through a public form that goes to an approval queue. Remind owners to recheck each entry every 12 months and flag stale entries.
Hard filters run first: no power and no generator, inside damage or flood zone, not ADA-accessible, not reachable.
Scoring is deterministic and explainable, with tenant-adjustable weights and documented defaults. Show what would change the top pick.
Show the top three with reasons and the excluded sites with why. A named person accepts, edits or rejects; log the decision and reason.
Feeding recommendations: stops, time windows, meal estimates, and setup notes on language, pets and emotional or spiritual care.
Partner setup uses each partner's declared assets and limits from its profile (e.g. two canteens, meals per hour, staff).
POD recommendations: type, site and first-72-hour supply estimates from the planning factors.
Suggest walk-up points where Census data shows high shares of households without a vehicle.
MARC recommendations: site, partner mix from the top needs, and interpreter languages from the reports.
Never invent capacity or availability. Show the age of every input and warn when it is stale.
Equity guardrail: report each recommendation's coverage by tract income, renter share and language, and flag recommendations that leave a high-need area uncovered.
Recommendations come from rules and optimization, not from a language model. AI may only draft the plain-language explanation, which must match the computed reasons (AIG-07).

Proactive resource discovery: on a tenant-set schedule (default weekly, daily during an active event), AI searches public sources for possible new resources (community centers, places of worship, schools, cooling and warming centers, food pantries, clinics, large parking lots) and for changes to registered ones (closed, moved, new hours). It drafts each candidate with its source links, fills in what it can confirm, marks what is unknown, and pre-checks it against the registry criteria. Candidates go to the administrator's review queue to qualify in or out; nothing is added, changed or removed without a human decision. Rejected candidates are remembered so they are not proposed again unless something changes.
A digest of new candidates and registry changes goes to the administrator by email or in the console; during an active event, high-value candidates near unmet need are raised immediately.

Role home screens: damage assessment teams (routes and FEMA matrix), canvassers and assisted-reporting volunteers (resident intake on the resident's behalf, CHN-06), NGO crews (assigned needs and completion), site leads (shelter, feeding stop or POD census and capacity), and hazard spotters (quick reports).

Works on volunteers' own phones and on issued devices. Issued devices are enrolled in device management with optional single-app mode. On personal phones, the app protects only its own data: encrypted app storage, PIN or biometric unlock, screenshots blocked on screens with personal details, and remote wipe of app data without touching anything else on the phone.

Check-in by scanning a QR code at staging or entering an event code. Check-in records the person, agency, team, credentials and start time; check-out ends the shift. This feeds accountability and the ICS 214 activity log automatically.
GPS drops a pin and snaps it to the nearest parcel or structure from county parcel data cached on the device, then asks "Is this the property?" with the parcel outline and address of record.

The volunteer can drag the pin, pick a different parcel, or add a landmark note. Records keep GPS accuracy, the parcel ID and a US National Grid coordinate, so search and rescue and FEMA teams can find the spot without an address.
Show cached pre-disaster imagery under the pin so a volunteer can match a destroyed home to its lot.
Photo-first capture: take photos, then tag them. Photos keep location and time internally and are stripped of metadata on export (PHO-06).
FEMA degree of damage chosen from pictures and short descriptions for the home type, never from definitions alone.
Voice notes: the AI drafts fields from what the volunteer said, and the volunteer confirms each one (INT-13).
Street sweep mode: walking a block, one tap per property (no damage, affected, minor, major, destroyed, can't reach), and the pin advances to the next parcel.
Quick report from any screen: hazard (downed line, gas, blocked road, unsafe structure), site status, or resource seen, as a pin, a photo and a category.
NGO crews mark a need done with a photo and note; canteen crews log meals served per stop; site leads update census and capacity in two taps.

Before deployment, the app downloads maps, parcels and assignments for the volunteer's area. Every record shows "On this phone," "Sending" or "Received"; sync happens on any connection; two records for the same property are flagged for a reviewer, never overwritten.
Volunteers see only their own assignments. Resident personal details are cleared from the device after sync and at check-out.
Built for field use: targets usable with gloves, high-contrast mode for sunlight, one-handed operation, and a battery saver that lowers location frequency.
Safety: a help button sends location and team to dispatch; warnings when entering a hazard area marked on the map; a check-in timer reminds the team lead (DSP-07).
No data relay over amateur radio. Positions or status heard on a radio net are entered by net control on the dispatch board (DSP-10).

Live operations map: checked-in people and teams by status (available, en route, on task, break, out of service, overdue), plus open needs, field routes, hazards, closures and open sites. A list view and filters by agency, skill, team and status sit beside it.

Resource roster: people, teams and units (e.g. Canteen 2, Chainsaw Team B) with agency, skills and credentials (damage assessor, chainsaw certified, Spanish speaker, chaplain, ham operator), equipment, shift times and hours worked.
Unassigned work queue: needs, verification routes, outreach tasks and site staffing gaps, sorted by priority.

Assign by dragging work onto a team or using the command window ("send the nearest chainsaw team to Willow Bend lot 41"). The console suggests the nearest qualified available team with reasons; a dispatcher confirms. Assignments go to the field app and need acknowledgement; unacknowledged after 10 minutes (tenant-set) raises an alert.
Status changes with one tap in the field app. The board suggests "arrived" or "left" from location, for the team to confirm.
Messages to a person, team, agency or map area, with templates and read receipts, and SMS fallback for people not using the app.

Safety: a check-in timer per team (default 60 minutes); a missed check-in turns the team "overdue" and alerts the dispatcher, then the safety officer. Help-button alerts take over the screen until acknowledged. Teams heading into a newly marked hazard area are warned.

Location is shared only while checked in, and the volunteer always sees that it is on. Positions are visible only to dispatch and safety roles, at a precision the tenant sets. Live position trails are kept 30 days by default; positions tied to incident records stay with the record.
Each agency dispatcher sees and assigns its own people; the county coordinator sees everyone; visibility is configurable by role, agency or person (CON-15).
Net control mode: a radio operator logs status and positions heard on ARES, RACES or agency nets against the right team, with an ICS 309-style communications log.
Every assignment, status change and message feeds the significant events log and each team's ICS 214 activity log.
Timeline replay of the board for briefings and after-action review.
The board is labeled as volunteer and resource coordination, not emergency dispatch. Anything that needs 911 goes to 911 (CON-10).

Every survivor gets a reference code and QR code: on their SMS confirmation, a printed card, or a shelter wristband. Scanning it opens their record for any worker the survivor has consented to. No ID is ever required. The code is always printed and sent as text too, so the QR code is never the only way in (ACC-50).
Without a code, a worker finds the record by phone number plus a one-time code sent to the survivor, or by address plus name, and the survivor confirms it is them.

One shared survivor record ("tell it once"): damage, needs, household, access needs, help received, referrals and appointments. Each organization sees only the sections the survivor consented to share with it (NED-03).

Conversation scribe: with the survivor's spoken or tapped consent, the app listens during a conversation and drafts a structured note: needs heard, help given, follow-ups and referrals. A visible "listening" indicator shows the whole time; the survivor can say stop. The worker reviews the draft afterward in under 30 seconds. Audio is deleted once the note is confirmed; only the confirmed note is kept.
The scribe is off by default for counseling, spiritual care, legal aid and anything involving a child, and cannot be turned on for counseling or spiritual care.
One-tap service logging: meal served, water case given, tarp installed, voucher issued, cot assigned, ride given. Counters work from a lock-screen widget and with gloves.
Voice commands for common actions ("log two meals," "refer to case management," "I'm done here"), always confirmed on screen before saving.
Smartwatch support for counters, check-in timers and help alerts.
Photos of documents a survivor chooses to share (lease, ID, insurance letter) go straight into their record with consent, never into the camera roll.

Warm referrals: with the survivor's consent, a worker refers them to another organization or role in two taps. The receiver is notified, the referral shows open, accepted or done, and the referrer sees when it closes.
The survivor gets plain-language SMS updates in their language ("A cleanup crew is scheduled for Tuesday morning") and can reply, so fewer people call the EOC.
Shift hand-over: when a worker checks out, AI drafts a summary of what happened and what is still open for the next shift, which the worker confirms.
Help received is logged with source, type and dollar value, so case managers can check for duplication of benefits before FEMA, SBA or other aid is given.

Live conversation translation between worker and survivor in the launch languages, labeled as machine translation, with one tap to bring in a human interpreter by phone or video. Consent, legal and medical conversations always use a human interpreter.
Offline job aids per role: checklists, FEMA damage matrices, shelter standards, food safety, child safeguarding and safety briefings.
Worker wellbeing: hours on shift, rest reminders after a tenant-set limit, and a private way to ask for peer support.
Volunteer hours and donated equipment are logged automatically from check-in and assignments, so the county can claim them as credit toward its share of FEMA Public Assistance costs.

Scribe launch safeguards: each tenant and each partner organization can turn the scribe on or off; the survivor's consent (spoken or tapped, in their language) is stored with the note; the scribe never runs in the background or without the indicator; audio is processed under the AI provider terms in AIG-06 and deleted after the note is confirmed; extraction accuracy is measured per language and the scribe turns itself off for a language whose correction rate crosses the tenant threshold (AIG-09).
Firefighters and rescue teams: Digital search marking per structure (searched, time, team, occupants, hazards), mirroring the spray-painted marks; a "searched" map layer so no block is searched twice
